response.answer: For complete metric spaces, unbounded curvature implies infinite diameter. Contraction and interface-estimation rates depend on dimension and curvature, with optimal rates for manifold estimation being O(n^(-k/d)). Theoretical proofs often break down for non-smooth or highly irregular spaces.

results.title: mg.metric geometry - Unbounded curvature implies infinite diameter on complete metric spaces - MathOverflow
results.content: # Unbounded curvature implies infinite diameter on complete metric spaces. I recently asked this question Unbounded sectional curvature implies infinite diameter?. So my question is: if the Alexandrov curvature of $(M,d)$ is not bounded from above, is the diameter of $(M,d)$ infinite? If you have a complete non-compact surface of finite diameter, you can always make a sequence of very little holes in it and glue in spheres of very large curvature. So the question is equivalent to: "does there exist a complete Riemannian manifold of finite diameter?" $\endgroup$. $\begingroup$ Could you say exactly what you mean by unbounded curvature of a metric space? $\begingroup$ The curvature of a (complete) metric space has no, at least obvious, meaning. Within certain classes, you'll find Alexandrov spaces as limits of Riemannian manifolds where certain curvature bounds make sense, but you need to formulate a more precise question to get a reasonable answer. * $\begingroup$ If the space (with a Riemannian metric) is complete but not compact, it must have infinite diameter. As a result we can say that the surface of the unit cube does have infinite curvature in the sense that it is not a $CAT(k)$ space for any finite $k$. * $\begingroup$ This isn't true of the only definition I know of curvature of a metric space -- viz, satisfying the $CAT(\kappa)$ condition for some $\kappa$. The surface of the unit cube is a $CAT(1)$ space. My intuition was that you could take a sequence of smooth manifolds starting at the sphere converging to the cube surface and then the entire curvature would accumulate in the corners. But the question is about metric spaces. * $\begingroup$ @HJRW No, the surface of a cube (with Euclidean metric on faces and with the geodesic metric) is not CAT$(\kappa)$ for any $\kappa<+\infty$. * $\begingroup$ @HJRW, curvature conditions on metric spaces is a vast subject (as you likely know): $CAT(\kappa)$, Alexandrov spaces and $\delta$-hyperbolicity are just some of the most well studied. Find the answer to your question by asking. 10") Alexandrov spaces which are not limits of Riemannian manifolds. Limit space of a sequence of Riemannian manifolds with uniformly bounded below Ricci curvature.

Title: Gingival shape analysis using surface curvature estimation of the intraoral scans | BMC Oral Health | Springer Nature Link
The method consists of four main steps, i.e., optical scanning, surface curvature estimation, region of interest (ROI) definition, and gingival shape analysis. Six different curvature measures and three different diameters were tested for surface curvature estimation on central (n = 78) and interdental ROI (n = 88) of patients with advanced periodontitis to quantify gingiva with a novel gingival shape parameter (GS). Surface curvature estimation of the intraoral optical scans presents a precise and highly reproducible method for the objective gingival shape quantification enabling the detection of subtle changes. Therefore, the present study aimed to propose an objective evaluation method for gingival shape analysis using surface curvature estimation of the intraoral optical scans by applying different curvature measures computed at various parameters on central and interdental gingiva. The proposed method consisted of four main steps, i.e., image acquisition—optical scanning, surface curvature estimation, region of interest (ROI) definition, and gingival shape analysis. Mean and standard deviation of gingival shape parameter (GS) (i.e., the 95th percentile of the curvature values)—light grey, and method error, i.e., the absolute difference in the GS between scan and rescan—dark grey, obtained for each diameter and curvature measure for a study sample represented with bar charts. The proposed method for gingival shape analysis using surface curvature estimation was demonstrated in a clinical case of periodontitis treatment (Figs. Evaluation of soft tissue dynamics associated with periodontitis treatment by volumetric assessment (**a**—baseline scan (T0), **b**—follow-up scan (T1), and **c**—colour-coded map) and a novel gingival shape analysis using surface curvature (**d**—T0 and T1 scans, **e**—mean curvature (MC) and **f**—minimum curvature (Min)). The surface curvature estimation of the intraoral scans presents a precise method for gingival shape analysis demonstrated by a high ratio of curvature values versus methodological error. Within the limitations of the present study, surface curvature estimation of the intraoral scans seems to be a precise and reproducible method for gingival shape analysis. Baseline (T0) and three-month follow-up (T1) after non-surgical periodontal treatment intraoral scans (upper row) were evaluated with gingival shape analysis using surface curvature using available curvature measures. *et al.* Gingival shape analysis using surface curvature estimation of the intraoral scans.
